highlights.title: NY Fed: Businesses Using AI to Transform Work, Not Cut Jobs
highlights.summary: Three years of NY Fed regional business surveys find that AI adoption is accelerating but firms are primarily redeploying workers rather than eliminating positions outright. The data suggest workforce transformation—task restructuring and upskilling—is the dominant near-term employer response to AI. This challenges displacement-centric narratives and points instead to within-firm labor reallocation (NY Fed Liberty Street Economics, September 2026).

highlights.title: Revelio RPLS: US Economy Adds Only 36.5k Jobs in August; AI-Exposed Occupations Weakening
highlights.summary: Revelio Public Labor Statistics recorded a sharply below-trend 36,500 net jobs added in August 2026, while active job postings declined a further 3%. Critically, Revelio's AI Labor Market Tracker shows employment deteriorating most in occupations with the highest AI exposure, suggesting early displacement pressure is concentrating in white-collar and routine cognitive roles. The divergence between aggregate resilience and occupation-level weakness is a key signal to watch (Revelio Labs, September 2026).

highlights.title: Fed FEDS Note: Publicly Available Indicators to Track the AI Buildout and Its Economic Impact
highlights.summary: Fed economists Soto, Thieu, and Allen catalogue publicly available, high-frequency indicators—covering capital expenditure, chip shipments, electricity demand, and labor market signals—that can be used to track the AI buildout in near-real time. The note provides a structured framework for policymakers to assess whether AI investment is translating into broader economic and productivity effects. It is among the most policy-relevant Fed publications on AI measurement to date (Federal Reserve Board FEDS Notes, July/September 2026).

highlights.title: AI Substitution vs. Complementarity: How Both Forces Drive Labor Market Polarization
highlights.summary: Using granular occupational task data and longitudinal employment trends, Li (2026) finds that AI simultaneously substitutes for routine cognitive tasks while complementing high-skill analytical work, producing a polarization effect that compresses middle-skill employment and widens the wage gap between top and bottom skill deciles. The study identifies a tipping threshold in task routineness beyond which substitution dominates complementarity. These findings have direct implications for entry-level and mid-career wage trajectories (OpenAlex, September 2026).

highlights.title: AI and the Screen Entertainment Industries: Value-Chain Disruption Across Film and TV
highlights.summary: Finney (2026) maps AI's integration across the screen entertainment value chain—from pre-production scripting tools through post-production VFX and distribution—finding that creative and technical mid-tier roles face the sharpest near-term displacement pressure. The book argues that AI is compressing production budgets and reducing demand for contract and freelance crew at scale. It represents one of the most comprehensive sector-level treatments of AI's creative-industry labor impact published this cycle (Routledge, September 2026).

themes: Workforce transformation over outright job cuts: Employer survey evidence (NY Fed) consistently shows AI driving task restructuring rather than mass layoffs—reallocation, not elimination, is the dominant near-term mechanism.

Occupation-level divergence beneath aggregate stability: Revelio RPLS data reveal that weak headline job growth in August 2026 masks sharper deterioration concentrated in high-AI-exposure white-collar occupations.

Polarization via dual substitution/complementarity: New task-based research confirms AI simultaneously hollows out middle-skill roles and amplifies returns to high-skill workers, accelerating wage divergence.

Creative and entertainment sectors entering acute displacement phase: Sector-specific analysis of screen industries documents budget compression and freelance demand destruction as AI tools penetrate the full production value chain.

Data infrastructure for AI impact tracking is maturing: The Fed's cataloguing of high-frequency AI buildout indicators signals that policymakers are moving from conceptual frameworks to real-time monitoring—raising the quality bar for future research.
